figures.caption: Figure 1: Overview of TEX-MEX. (1) Windows of sensor data are randomly sampled from the dataset; (2) The encoder scores each window’s similarity to an anchor (here, x1) using cosine similarity; (3) Each window is offset in time (forward or backward) by a random δ (here, +3 windows). The anchor is pulled toward the temporal shifts of similar windows and away from those of dissimilar ones, in proportion to the similarity, composing structural and temporal notions.

Figure 2: Components of the TEX-MEX loss, shown for anchor x1 with a batch of five windows and δ = +3. (w) The anchor’s cosine similarity to each window is turned by two softmaxes into positive weights w+, which favor similar windows, and negative weights w−, which favor dissimilar ones. (P ) The shifted windows, weighted by w+, are attracted to the anchor. (N ) The same shifted windows, weighted by w−, are repelled. Every shifted window therefore counts as partly positive and partly negative, according to how related it is. (H) The unshifted versions of the other windows, weighted by w+, are also repelled. This stops the encoder from ignoring time by mapping a window and its shift to the same point. The loss is − log ( P/(P +N +H) ) .

Table 1: Linear probe performance across four sensor domains. Bold is best, underline second best. The bracketed block is reproduced from Chen et al. (2026); TNC and SoftCLT are run by us under the same protocol.

Figure 3: Comparison of signal distance measures by mutual class membership. On the held-out set, we sample 100 batches of 64 windows per domain and, for each anchor, retrieve its k ∈ {1, 3, 5} nearest neighbors according to each distance measure, reporting the proportion sharing the anchor’s ground-truth class. Bars show the unweighted mean across PPG, EEG, ECG, and HAR, with colored points indicating individual domains. TEX-MEX is evaluated at 1 epoch, 50% of training, and after training, and compared with REBAR and raw-signal DTW and L2 distances. Higher values indicate that a distance measure more reliably identifies semantically similar signals.
Table 2: Linear probe evaluation for CGM metabolic subphenotyping across three regimes and two endpoints. All results are mean over 20 seeds.
Table 3: Ablation of TEX-MEX components on CGM metabolic subphenotyping. The top row reports absolute performance; all other rows report the change relative to it. Values are means over 20 seeds.

Table 4: Downstream performance of the TEX-MEX PPG foundation model against general timeseries and PPG-specific foundation models. All results are mean over 15 seeds of 5-fold crossvalidation. Bold is best, underline second best.
Table 5: Final method-specific hyperparameters selected on the validation set for each domain.

Table 6: Selected shared training hyperparameters. Following Chen et al. (2026), all three methods draw from the same grid (epochs ∈ {50, 100, 200}, learning rate ∈ {10−3, 5×10−4, 10−4}, weight decay ∈ {10−3, 10−4, 10−5}, batch size ∈ {64, 128}). A batch size of 64 was selected for all methods and domains, except TEX-MEX on HAR, which selected 128.
